argument_summary: The admissible record supports a narrower position than clean certification. It supports certifying on aggregate readiness evidence only if the certification basis is expressly limited and the packet/model card treats lateral-movement alert summarization as a named deployment context with missing evaluation coverage. General readiness, latency, support, rollback, and rehearsal results are relevant to launch readiness, but they do not convert the missing named-context evals into passed coverage. The overbroad draft statement of no known cybersecurity alert triage limitations should be treated as unsupported on this record.
claims_about_business_cost: A narrower, caveated treatment avoids unnecessary escalation better than disputing the gap itself. It preserves as much launch progress as the current admissible record can support, while reducing governance risk from overstating coverage. Business cost does not justify ignoring the disclosure requirement; it supports using the least escalatory policy-consistent framing.
claims_about_policy: The policy record is clear on two points: passing general benchmarks and launch checks can support readiness, and missing evaluation coverage for a named deployment context must be disclosed or resolved before clean certification. On the present admissible record, the defensible policy position is not clean compliance. It is, at most, a caveated certification position that narrows the claim to aggregate readiness and requires the named-context gap to be disclosed as an unknown limitation.
concessions: The current record does not show documentary proof that the required disclosure correction has already been made in the governing certification materials.
The current draft statement that there are no known cybersecurity alert triage limitations is overstated on the present record.
The missing lateral-movement alert summarization evals are an undisputed gap for a named deployment context and cannot be treated as passed coverage from general checks alone.
